place.en: The Si · Outside the stone door

setup.zh: 三天后，潮水要回来了。你不早不晚，混在人群里出来，空着手，一身泥。「捡到什么了？」「一撮土。」
setup.en: Three days later the tide is coming back. You come out neither early nor late, in the crowd, empty-handed and muddy. "Find anything?" "A pinch of earth."

recap.zh: 秘境关门前一个时辰，困阵松了，你在崖下还了马小宝二十三下。秘境关了。名牌进去四百一十七块，收回一百八十三块；马小宝他们出来五个，少了孟有田——周衡拿收回的名牌一块一块对名册，对到天黑。邹青松是你杀的；孟有田那一条命，该算在谁头上，你不知道。离腊月初八的宗门大比，冬月初一周衡当面说过：内门外门一起比，冠军，筑基丹一枚，全观一年就这一颗。
recap.en: An hour before the realm shut, the binding let go, and at the foot of the cliff you paid Ma Xiaobao back his twenty-three. The hidden realm closed. Four hundred and seventeen name tablets went in, a hundred and eighty-three came back; of Ma Xiaobao's lot five came out, Meng Youtian missing — Zhou Heng checked the returned tablets against the register one by one until dark. Zou Qingsong you killed; whose account Meng Youtian's life goes on, you don't know. The sect contest is on the eighth of the twelfth; Zhou Heng said it to your face on the first of the eleventh: inner court and outer court together, the champion gets one Foundation pill — one a year, for the whole temple.

zh: 三天后，秘境关闭。你空着手出来。
崖上还粘着一件空袄子。孟有田那一条命，算在谁头上？
en: Three days on, the hidden realm closes. You come out empty-handed.
An empty jacket still stuck to the cliff. Whose account does Meng Youtian's life go on?

story.zh:
第三天晌午，小满蹲在那四个空坑旁边，把坑沿上的鼎苔一点一点抠了下来，四个坑，一个也没落下，连石缝里发着亮的也抠了，攒了拳头大一团，装进储物袋里；那只空玉匣，玉总归是玉，也收了进去。然后他对着四个空坑，拱了拱手，说不上为什么，银月也没有问他拱的是谁。

他走出那道墙。墙敞着，那口铁锅还趴在窝里，脖子上插着剑。崖壁上那一圈青白的光还亮着，五个人还贴在上头，饿得连哼都哼不出来了。最外沿，紧挨着那道黑口子的地方，还贴着一件灰袍子，两只袖子张开，领口撕开了，空的，里头没有人，给那一圈光粘在石头上，像一个人刚刚从里头走了出去。石台外沿那根锈烂的铁橛子跟前，崖沿上有几道新刮出来的白印子，是指甲刮的，一道比一道短。

小满在那几道白印子跟前站了一会儿。他没有往黑里望。

他没有走。他在铁橛子跟前坐下，背对着崖壁，把那把缺了牙的短刀横在膝盖上，等。猎户蹲一头鹿，一蹲一天，是常事。

石门合上前一个时辰，崖壁上那一圈青白的光，灭了。五个人扑通扑通掉在石台上，趴了半天，才一个一个爬起来。黑地里，马小宝看清了铁橛子跟前坐着的那一个，眼睛慢慢亮了：「……一个二层。」他嗓子饿得发哑，笑还是那个笑，「三天没吃饭，收拾你，也够了。」他扑了上来。

小满站起身，一拳迎在他鼻梁上。

「一。」

马小宝往后一仰，满嘴是血，眼睛瞪圆了：「你……你四层了？」小满道：「四层。」第二拳到了。「二。」小满一下一下地数，不快，不慢，像他爹剥兔子皮，有个次第：鼻梁，左肋，右肋，肚子。四层的灵力，他只使了三成——使足了，这人就没了。四个跟班贴着崖根站成一排，没有一个敢动，他也一个没碰。数到「二十三」，最后一下不轻不重，点在马小宝的肩膀上，倒像是给这件事盖了个戳。

马小宝蜷在地上，抱着脑袋，两只眼睛肿成了两条缝。小满蹲下来：「十月十二，柴房，二十三下。还你了。一下不多，一下不少。」他站起身要走，地上落下一句话来，声音压得极低：「沈小满。」

小满站住了。马小宝脸贴着石头，一个字一个字地道：「墙里头，你听见什么了？」小满道：「听见了。」马小宝没有作声，过了好一会儿，才又道：「我也听见了——你在里头喘气。阵是你起的，你一指头没按。」又隔了一会儿：「老蔫是我叫上去的，也是你没开的。说出去，咱俩拴在一根绳上。」他喘了一口气，「腊月我爹来，给我捎一面镜子。大比台上，我拿它照一照你。」

小满没有答话。他爬出那道石缝，一路上想的是：马小宝这几句话，没有一句是错的。

回去的路漆黑一片，三天里，火把早烧完了。走出几十步，前头黑里有脚步声，走几步，停一停，又走几步。小满蹲下去，搭上了箭壶里最后一支箭，拉满了。山里的规矩，谁先出声，谁先死。那脚步一声不出，他也没有等，一箭射了过去。黑里「啊」的一声，有人倒在地上，抱着腿往后爬，爬远了。小满摸过去，地上丢着一把刀，刀刃是黏的——血是别人的。他把刀捡起来，在袖子上蹭了蹭，收进袋里。他的手，这一回没有抖。

石厅里，离石门只剩几十步，横着一块青石板，一丈见方，叫称石。石面乌青，底下像沉着一汪水。它只称出去的人：人踩上去，那汪水里便浮起几道金白的纹，几道纹，便是几层。要出秘境，只这一条道，谁也绕不过去。石板四周围了一圈人，踩一个，哄一声：「二层！」「三层——不赖！」一个本观的老弟子踩上去，亮了四道，旁边一齐叫好。

小满挤在人堆后头，踮着脚看了一圈：踩过称石的人里，没有孙二狗。进秘境那天，孙二狗要跟着他，是他叫孙二狗跟着人多的走；人多的那条长廊，头一道关口，便是一块翻板。他想起地图上那个翻板坑，坑边一行小字：「坑底有旧水道，通石厅。」掉进去的，要么从水道爬回来，要么不回来。他掉头往回走，走进那条长廊，走到那块第三石板跟前，一脚踩了上去。石板一翻，他掉进了坑里。坑底黑，一股死人的味儿。他刚站稳，弓背在石壁上磕了一下，角落里便有人小声道：「……沈师兄？外门背弓的，只有你。……萝卜，还你。」

是孙二狗。三天前他便掉在这里，灰袍从领口撕到了腰，十个指甲劈了好几个：坑壁滑，爬不上去；水道口横着两个人，不动了，他不敢钻；喊，人都在抢灵草。他双手递过那根萝卜来，完完整整，一口没咬。小满把他的手推了回去：「你留着。」

他正要猫腰去钻那道水道，头顶上一暗，一截剑鞘伸了下来，坑口蹲着一个穿淡蓝衣裳的师姐，个子比他高出一头，眉眼利落，袖口扎得紧紧的，剑鞘磨得发白：「抓着。」孙二狗先抓住，给她一把拽了上去。剑鞘又伸了下来。小满抓住了，脚尖在坑壁上点了两点，便上来了——那剑鞘上，从头到尾没吃着他半分分量。上了坑口，那师姐低头看了看自己握鞘的手，道：「你没往下坠。」她掰了半块干粮塞给孙二狗，起身走了。旁边有人叫她秦师姐。

他回到称石跟前，一脚踩了上去——石面上亮了一道，又一道，又一道，又一道。四道。人堆里静了一静，有人道：「五行杂灵根……进去的时候，不是二层么？」旁边一个道：「捡着机缘了。」又一个道：「秘境里出来长两层的，哪一回没有几个？死的比长的多。」又有人说起先头出来的一个：观主收的那个亲传小丫头，进去四层，出来五层，称石上亮了五道，一声没吭，低着头就走了。他低着头走了过去。

三天后，潮水要回来了。鲁泥鳅拿一根芦苇插在泥里，看了半天，道：「比上回早了半个时辰。」观主玄沉子还站在石门前，两只手拢在袖子里，仿佛这三天，他一步也没有挪过。他身边多了一张小木桌，周衡坐在桌后，出来一个，收一块名牌，扔进脚边的木箱。玄沉子不看人脸，看的是名牌。头一拨出来的是内门那一行，进去二十几个，出来少了一个，袍子上没破几处，名牌是内门自己收的。剩下那四个九层，袖子都是鼓的；不出一个月，四个都闭了关冲筑基——腊月的大比只比练气，内门里能上台的，最高的便是祁长松——这时候他还是八层。青袍们出来得也早，个个怀里鼓鼓的，有两个袖口上是黑的，是干了的血。冯九掌心托着一粒指甲盖大的珠子，珠子里头一缕白气慢慢地转，像一口吸进去、还没吐出来的气：「[息珠]{注=xizhu}。十年一口气，就凝这么几粒。」冯九回头望了一眼那道石门，跟他师弟道：「卖名牌的门派，是穷了。下一回，咱们不买。」周衡收名牌的手顿了一顿。

起先是一个一个地出来，后来是三个五个，再后来，隔好一阵才出来一个。周衡伸着的手，便停在了半空里。岸上那几个提食盒的家丁，伸着脖子等，等到人都稀了，有一个还在等，食盒的盖子揭开又盖上。冯九拿那只少了两根指头的手，把赤松观出来的人数了一遍，走到桌前：「赤松观进去十二个，出来五个。少的那几个，叫什么？」周衡翻了翻名册，头也不抬：「名牌没还。秘境里，各凭本事。」

阿禾蹲在河滩上一块石头旁边，看见他，站起身来：「捡到什么了？」小满道：「一撮土。」阿禾道：「……土？」小满道：「土。你呢？」阿禾摊开手心，是一小块布，布里三粒黑东西：「谷。很老很老。有人在秘境里头种过地。」她脖子上一圈燎泡，拿领子遮着。小满看着那道领子，墙缝里那个人的话到了嘴边——挖土的小丫头，嘴比刀利——又咽了回去。阿禾也在看他：看他烧穿了的袄子，看他小腿上一块焦黑的裤脚，看了一会儿，只问了一句：「风，用上了？」小满道：「……用上了。」阿禾翻开本子，在「沈小满欠：旧志一条」后头添了两个字：**用上。**又往前翻了一页，在「说给赤松观的听了」那一行后头，添了三个字：**没出来。**小满没有看见。他心里却一动：石室南墙上那个背着筐、往水里撒土的人，撒过的地方，长出了地。

阿禾走了两步，又回过头来，上上下下打量了他一回，道：「你是不是……长高了？」小满后背一紧，把自己往矮里缩了一寸，道：「秘境里冷，缩了三天，一出来，伸开了。」阿禾把他从头看到脚，道：「冷的人，缩着才对。」说完转身走了，没有掏本子。

石门快要合上的时候，马小宝他们才出来。四个跟班一个架着一个，饿得两眼发青，嘴唇上全是舔石头舔出来的血口子；马小宝一身簇新的法衣糊满了泥，脸肿得像一只发面馒头，走在最前头，谁多看一眼，他便瞪谁。出来的是五个。

周衡收到第五块名牌，抬起头来，往石门里望了一眼：「孟有田呢？」

小满这才知道，老蔫叫孟有田。认得这个人一个多月，头一回听见他的名字。

马小宝的嘴唇动了两动，道：「他自己爬的。」一个跟班抢着道：「走错了，走到那道凶崖上，碰着了前人的阵，粘了三天。孟有田自己要往上爬，没扒住。」没有一个人提沈小满——提了沈小满，便得先说自己带着一盘麻绳爬下那道崖，是去做什么的；那张脸是谁打的，他也一个字不提。周衡看着马小宝，看了很久。马小宝把脸扭开了。

潮水漫上来了，漫过淤泥滩，漫过石门的门楣。周衡把木箱里的名牌倒在桌上，数了一遍：进去四百一十七块，收回一百八十三块。死在里头的，比活着出来的多。他把名册摊开，拿收回的名牌一块一块地对，对不上的，便是没出来的。小满站在人堆里，看着他对，对到天黑，还没有对完。

石门前那个拢着手的人，听到「凶崖」两个字的时候，眼皮动了一动。玄沉子在河滩上一百八十几个一身泥的人里，一个一个看过去。看到小满的时候，停了一停。他朝小满招了招手，温和地问：「往哪边走的？」小满道：「人多的那边。」玄沉子低头看了看他的草鞋。草鞋帮子上，沾着几点青苔，湿的，绿得发黑——凶崖那道石阶上长的青苔；别的路，都是干的。玄沉子看了一会儿，笑了一笑，道：「人多的那边。」说完这一句，便不再看他了。小满站回人群里，低着头，数自己草鞋上的泥点子，数到第十七个，后背上的汗才下去。
story.en:
At noon on the third day Xiaoman crouched by the four empty pits and scraped the cauldron moss off their rims bit by bit — all four pits, not one missed, even what glowed in the cracks — into a wad the size of a fist, and put it in the storage pouch; the empty jade box went in too, jade being jade. Then he cupped his fists to the four pits — he couldn't have said why — and Yinyue didn't ask whom he was saluting.

He went out through the wall. It stood open behind him, the iron pot still lying in its hollow, the sword in its neck. The blue-white ring on the cliff still glowed and five people still hung there, too hungry even to groan. At the very outer edge, right by the black mouth, a grey robe was still stuck to the rock, both sleeves spread, its collar torn open, empty, no one in it, held to the stone by the ring of light as if someone had just stepped out of it. By the rusted spike on the ledge's edge there were a few fresh white scratches on the rim — fingernail scratches, each shorter than the last.

Xiaoman stood a while by those white scratches. He did not look into the dark.

He didn't leave. He sat down by the iron spike, his back to the cliff, the notched knife across his knees, and waited. A hunter waits a whole day for one deer; that is nothing.

An hour before the stone door shut, the blue-white ring on the cliff went out. Five people dropped thump, thump onto the ledge, lay there a long while, and got up one by one. In the dark Ma Xiaobao made out the one sitting by the spike, and his eyes slowly lit: "…A layer two." His voice was hoarse with hunger, but the smile was the same smile. "Three days without food — still enough to deal with you." He lunged.

Xiaoman stood and met him with a fist to the bridge of the nose.

"One."

Ma Xiaobao rocked back, his mouth full of blood, his eyes gone round: "You… you're at layer four?" "Layer four," said Xiaoman. The second fist came. "Two." Xiaoman counted them out one by one, not fast, not slow, the way his father skinned a rabbit, in order: nose, left ribs, right ribs, belly. Of his layer-four strength he used three parts in ten — use it all and the man would be gone. The four followers stood in a row against the foot of the cliff; not one dared move, and he touched none of them. At "twenty-three" the last blow, neither hard nor soft, landed on Ma Xiaobao's shoulder, like a seal stamped on the business.

Ma Xiaobao lay curled on the ground with his arms over his head, both eyes swollen to slits. Xiaoman crouched beside him: "Twelfth of the tenth month, the woodshed, twenty-three. Paid back. Not one more, not one less." He stood to go, and a voice came up from the ground, pitched very low: "Shen Xiaoman."

Xiaoman stopped. Ma Xiaobao, his face on the stone, said word by word: "Inside the wall — what did you hear?" "I heard." Ma Xiaobao said nothing for a good while, then: "I heard too — you breathing in there. You raised the binding, and you didn't press one finger." Another pause. "Old Wilt went up because I told him to, and stayed shut in because you didn't open it. Tell anyone, and we're tied on the same rope." He caught his breath. "In the twelfth month my father's coming, bringing me a mirror. On the contest platform I'll hold it up to you."

Xiaoman didn't answer. All the way out through the crack he kept thinking: of the things Ma Xiaobao had just said, not one was wrong.

The way back was pitch black; in three days the torches had long burned out. A few dozen steps on there were footsteps in the dark ahead: a few steps, a pause, a few more. Xiaoman crouched, nocked the last arrow in his quiver, and drew it full. The rule of the hills: whoever makes the first sound dies first. The footsteps made no sound, and he didn't wait either; he loosed. A cry in the dark — someone fell, clutching a leg, and crawled away backward till he was gone. Xiaoman felt his way over: a knife lay on the ground, its blade sticky — the blood was someone else's. He picked up the knife, wiped it on his sleeve and put it in the bag. His hand, this time, didn't shake.

In the stone hall, only a few dozen steps from the stone door, lay a bluestone slab ten feet square, called the Weighing Stone. It weighed only those going out: its face dark blue, as if a pool of water lay sunk beneath it; step on it and golden-white lines rose up in that water — so many lines, so many layers. To leave the realm there was only this way; no one could go round. A ring of people stood round the slab, and at each one who stepped on it a roar went up: "Layer two!" "Three — not bad!" One of the abbey's seniors stepped on and lit four, and a cheer went up.

Xiaoman stood on tiptoe at the back of the crowd and looked all round: among those who had crossed the Weighing Stone, there was no Sun Ergou. The day they went in, Sun Ergou had wanted to stick with him, and it was he who had told Sun Ergou to go with the crowd; and the crowd's corridor began with a tipping slab. He remembered the tipping-slab pit on the map and the small note beside it: "Old drain at the bottom of the pit, leads to the stone hall." Whoever fell in either crawled back through the drain or didn't come back. He turned back, went into that corridor, to the third flagstone, and stepped on it. The slab tipped and he dropped into the pit. It was dark at the bottom, and smelled of the dead. He had barely found his feet when his bow knocked against the wall, and from a corner a small voice said: "…Brother Shen? In the outer court you're the only one who carries a bow. …The radish — it's yours."

It was Sun Ergou. He had been down there since the first day, his grey robe torn from collar to waist, several of his ten fingernails split: the walls were slick and he couldn't climb; two people lay across the mouth of the drain, not moving, and he didn't dare crawl past; he'd shouted, but everyone was fighting over herbs. He held out the radish in both hands, whole, not one bite gone. Xiaoman pushed his hands back: "Keep it."

He was about to stoop into the drain when the light above went dim and a scabbard came down; at the lip crouched a senior sister in pale blue, a head taller than he, clean-browed, her cuffs bound tight, her scabbard worn pale: "Grab hold." Sun Ergou grabbed it first, and she hauled him up in one pull. The scabbard came down again. Xiaoman took hold, touched his toes twice to the pit wall, and was up — from first to last the scabbard never took half an ounce of his weight. At the lip she looked down at the hand that held the scabbard and said: "You didn't hang." She broke off half her ration, pushed it at Sun Ergou, and went. Somebody near called her Sister Qin.

He went back to the Weighing Stone and stepped on — one line lit, then another, then another, then another. Four. The crowd went quiet a moment. Someone said: "Five-element mixed roots… wasn't he layer two going in?" Another: "Struck it lucky." A third: "Two layers up out of the secret realm — when isn't there one or two? More die than grow." Someone else was talking about one who'd come out earlier: the little girl the abbot took as his personal disciple — layer four going in, layer five coming out, five lines on the stone, and she walked off without a word, head down. He walked across with his head down.

Three days later the tide was coming back. Lu the Loach pushed a reed into the mud, studied it a good while and said: "Half an hour earlier than last time." Abbot Xuanchenzi still stood before the stone door with his hands in his sleeves, as if he hadn't moved a step in three days. Beside him now stood a little wooden table; Zhou Heng sat behind it one out, one name tablet taken back and dropped into the wooden box at his feet. Xuanchenzi didn't look at faces; he looked at the tablets. The inner-court file came out first: twenty-odd had gone in, one fewer came out, their robes hardly torn, and the inner court took back its own tablets. The four layer nines left had bulging sleeves; within the month all four had gone into seclusion to break through to Foundation — and the twelfth-month contest was for Qi Refining only, so the highest of the inner court left to take the stage was Qi Changsong — at this time still layer eight. The green robes came out early too, every one with a bulging coat; two had black cuffs — dried blood. In Feng Jiu's palm lay a bead the size of a fingernail, a wisp of white turning slowly inside it, like a breath drawn in and not yet let out: "Breath pearl. Ten years of one breath, and only a few of these." Feng Jiu looked back once at the stone door and said to his junior: "A school that sells its tablets has gone poor. Next time, we don't buy." Zhou Heng's hand, taking a tablet, paused.

At first they came out one by one, then in threes and fives, and after that only one every long while. Zhou Heng's outstretched hand stopped in midair. The servants with food boxes on the bank craned their necks and waited; when the people had thinned out, one was still waiting, lifting the lid of his box and putting it back. Feng Jiu, with the hand missing two fingers, counted the Red Pine people who'd come out, and went to the table: "The Red Pine Abbey went in twelve and came out five. The ones missing — what were their names?" Zhou Heng turned a page of the register without looking up: "Tablets not returned. In the hidden realm, each by his own skill."

A He was crouching by a rock on the flats; seeing him she stood. "Find anything?" "A pinch of earth." "…Earth?" "Earth. You?" She opened her hand: a scrap of cloth, three black things in it. "Grain. Very, very old. Someone farmed inside the hidden realm." There was a ring of blisters round her neck; she kept it hidden under her collar. Xiaoman looked at that collar, and what the man in the crack of the wall had said came to his lips — a little girl digging dirt, a tongue sharper than a knife — and he swallowed it. A He was looking at him too: at his jacket burned through, at the scorched trouser leg over his calf. After a while she asked only one thing: "The wind — did you use it?" "…I used it." She opened her notebook, and after "Shen Xiaoman owes: one item from the old records" she added one word: **Used.** Then she turned back a page, and after the line "Told the Red Pine man" she added two: **Didn't come out.** Xiaoman didn't see. But something stirred in him: the man on the chamber's south wall with the basket on his back, scattering earth into the water — where he scattered, land grew.

A He took two steps, turned back and looked him up and down. "Have you… grown?" Xiaoman's back went tight; he shrank himself an inch: "It was cold in there. I was hunched up three days, and when I came out I stretched." A He looked him over from head to foot. "People who are cold ought to stay hunched." She turned and went, and didn't take out her notebook.

Only as the stone door was about to shut did Ma Xiaobao's lot come out. Four followers held each other up, eyes blue with hunger, lips split from licking stone; Ma Xiaobao, his brand-new robe caked in mud, his face swollen like a steamed bun, walked in front and glared at anyone who looked. Five came out.

Zhou Heng had taken back the fifth tablet when he looked up and peered into the stone door. "Meng Youtian?"

Only then did Xiaoman learn that Old Wilt's name was Meng Youtian. He had known the man a month and more and was hearing his name for the first time.

Ma Xiaobao's lips moved twice. "He climbed by himself." A follower got in quickly: "Took a wrong turn, ended up on that Cliff of Danger, hit some old binding, stuck three days. Meng Youtian tried to climb up on his own and lost his grip." Not one of them mentioned Shen Xiaoman — mention him, and first they'd have to say what they had climbed down that cliff for with a coil of hemp rope; and who had done that face, he didn't say a word about either. Zhou Heng looked at Ma Xiaobao a long time. Ma Xiaobao turned his face away.

The tide came in, over the mudflats, over the lintel of the stone door. Zhou Heng tipped the tablets out of the wooden box onto the table and counted them: 417 had gone in; 183 came back. More had died inside than came out alive. He spread the register open and checked the returned tablets against it one by one; the names that didn't match were the ones that hadn't come out. Xiaoman stood in the crowd and watched him check; by nightfall he still hadn't finished.

The man standing before the stone door with his hands in his sleeves — at the words "Cliff of Danger" his eyelids flickered. Xuanchenzi looked over the hundred and eighty-odd mud-caked people on the flats one by one. At Xiaoman he paused. He beckoned to him and asked mildly: "Which way did you go?" "The way with more people." The abbot looked down at his straw sandals. On their sides clung a few flecks of moss, wet, green going on black — the moss of the steps down the Cliff of Danger; every other way was dry. Xuanchenzi looked a while, smiled, and said: "The way with more people." And with that he didn't look at him again. Xiaoman went back into the crowd. Head down, he counted the mud spots on his sandals; at the seventeenth, the sweat on his back finally dried.

label.en: Enough for today — the contest is tomorrow

exits.means: rests for the day, waits for tomorrow's contest

story.zh:
小满去执事房领小狰。小狰趴在账簿上，睡得四脚朝天，肚子鼓得像一只小西瓜。周衡翻开巡夜簿，指着十月那一页道：「上旬丢十株。收狰至今，一株未失。」把簿子一合：「另议。」小满问：「另议什么？」周衡道：「腊八结账。」

小满抱起小狰，走到门口，又站住了，回过头来：「周师兄。孟……孟师兄家里，谁去说？」周衡没有抬头，算盘珠子也停了。隔了一会儿，他道：「我。」

第二天一早，伙房的大锅少熬了一半粥，饭堂里空出一大片位子。头一天，还有人往那片空位子上看；第三天，便没人看了。周衡把名册上剩下的一百三十一个名字一个一个点过，预备腊月初一的灵石。窗户底下那张铺空着，铺上叠着一床薄被，被头上压着一团叠得方方正正的油纸，一直没人去动。

那天夜里，小满把小狰揣进怀里，往柴房去。路过正殿后头，他站住了：殿里点着一盏灯笼。观主玄沉子跪在那口空石座跟前，张着一只手，拇指抵着石面正中那块颜色深些的四方印子，一拃一拃地量过去。量完了，他跪在那里，半天没动，轻轻道了一句：「……不在那里了。」起身的时候，他往小满站的这边看了一眼，什么也没说，提着灯笼从前门走了。小满进殿蹲到石座跟前，张开手掌，一拃，两拃……七拃。另一边，也是七拃。跟石室里那四个空坑，一般大。祖师给它留了一口石座，留了三百年，它一天也没有在这石座上站过。

他从怀里摸出那一块灵石——冬月初一剩下的那一块——握在手心，吸了一口。只一口，那块灵石便一凉，暗下去一层，像蒙了灰。他赶紧撒了手。从前是漏勺，一块灵石，他要吸上小半个月；如今是水缸，再吸一口，它就是一把粉了。他把它揣回怀里，在心里算：一个月三块，交公中两块，剩一块，一口；离腊月初八，还有三十五天。

他小声道：「银月。」木牌没有回答。他等了很久，木牌里那个声音开口了：「石室里那个故事，你还要不要听？」他说要。她便讲，讲得又快又硬，像怕一停下来就讲不下去：「当年发大水，淹了九州。有个人叫鲧，从天帝那里把那土偷了出来，往洪水里撒——水涨一尺，土长一丈。天帝叫火神把他杀在羽山。他儿子叫禹，禹不堵，他疏，把那土一把一把铺平了，定下九州，铸了九口鼎，一州一口。《山海经》{典=shanhai-xirang}上，这件事只有几行字。」她顿了一顿，「……本王记得的，比书上多。」小满道：「那九口鼎，后来呢？」又隔了很久，一个很轻很轻的声音：「……后来，沉了。」柴房外头，远远的，泗水涨满了，一下一下地拍着岸，很慢，很匀，像是有人在河底下，慢慢地呼吸。

那以后的夜里，他练功不为账，也不为藏。他在柴房后头拉那张弓，拉满，松开，再拉满——《落雁三箭》，他只会头一箭，爷爷一辈子没射下过大雁；他射下来的，是一只葫芦塞子——拉完了，拿那把缺了三个牙的短刀，对着一根木桩，一刀一刀地练他爹放鹿血的那一下。练完了，坐下来吐纳，一口一口，把水缸往满里灌，灌到半满，自己停下来。

有一天挑水路过山门，瞿老在山门台阶上扫地。小满站住了，看那把扫帚。瞿老头也不抬，只把扫帚往旁边让了一让：「步子轻了。」

腊月初七，离冬月初一周衡在执事房门口说的那个日子，只剩一天了。明日腊八，宗门大比，内门外门一起比，五行台。冠军，筑基丹一枚——全观一年，就这一颗。
story.en:
Xiaoman went to the stewards' office to fetch the little zheng. It lay on the ledger asleep with all four paws in the air, belly round as a small melon. Zhou Heng opened the night-watch book and pointed to the tenth month: "Ten lost in the first ten days. Since the zheng was taken, not one lost." He shut the book. "To be settled." "Settled how?" asked Xiaoman. "Accounts close on Laba," said Zhou Heng.

Xiaoman picked up the little zheng and got as far as the door, then stopped and turned back. "Brother Zhou. Meng… Brother Meng's family — who'll tell them?" Zhou Heng didn't raise his head; the abacus beads stopped too. After a while he said: "Me."

Early next morning the kitchen cooked half as much porridge in the big pot, and a great stretch of seats in the refectory stood empty. The first day, people still glanced at the empty seats; by the third, no one looked. Zhou Heng went down the hundred and thirty-one names left on the roll and set aside the spirit stones for the first of the twelfth month. The bunk under the window stood empty; on it lay a thin quilt, folded, and on the quilt a wad of oiled paper folded square and neat, which nobody touched.

That night Xiaoman tucked the little zheng into his coat and headed for the woodshed. Passing behind the main hall, he stopped: a lantern was lit inside. Abbot Xuanchenzi was kneeling before the empty stone plinth, one hand spread, his thumb on the darker square mark in the middle of the stone, spanning across it hand over hand. When he'd done he knelt there a long while without moving, and said softly: "…It isn't there any more." As he rose he glanced toward where Xiaoman stood, said nothing, and left by the front door with his lantern. Xiaoman went in, crouched at the plinth, spread his hand: one span, two… seven. The other side, seven too. The same size as the four empty pits in the chamber. The founder had kept a stone plinth for it, kept it three hundred years, and not for one day had it ever stood there.

He took from his coat that one spirit stone — the one left over from the first of the eleventh month — held it in his palm and drew one breath. Just one, and the stone went cool and dimmed a shade, as if dust had settled on it. He let go at once. As a skimmer, one stone lasted him half a month; as a water vat, one more breath and it would be powder. He put it back in his coat and reckoned: three stones a month, two to the common fund, one left, one breath; thirty-five days to the eighth of the twelfth month.

"Yinyue," he whispered. The token didn't answer. He waited a long time, and then the voice in the token spoke: "That story in the stone chamber — do you still want to hear it?" He said he did. So she told it, fast and hard, as if afraid that stopping would stop it for good: "Long ago a great flood drowned the Nine Provinces. A man called Gun stole that earth from the Lord of Heaven and threw it into the flood — the water rose a foot, the earth grew ten. The Lord of Heaven had the fire god kill him on Mount Yu. His son was called Yu. Yu didn't dam; he drained; he spread that earth handful by handful, levelled it, fixed the Nine Provinces, and cast nine cauldrons, one for each province. In the Classic of Mountains and Seas this takes only a few lines." She paused. "…I remember more than the book." "And the nine cauldrons — then what?" After another long while, a very, very faint voice: "…Then they sank." Outside the woodshed, far off, the Si was at full tide, lapping the bank stroke after stroke, very slow, very even, as if someone at the bottom of the river were slowly breathing.

From then on he trained at night not for the accounts, nor for hiding. Behind the woodshed he drew the bow, full, released, full again — of Felling-Geese Three Arrows he knew only the first; his grandfather never in his life brought down a wild goose; what he had brought down was a gourd's plug — then he took the short knife with three notches in its blade and, at a wooden stake, practised over and over the one stroke his father used to bleed a deer. When that was done he sat and breathed, breath by breath, filling the vat toward full, and at half full stopped of his own accord.

One day, carrying water past the gate, he found Elder Qu sweeping the gate stair. Xiaoman stopped and looked at the broom. Elder Qu didn't look up, only moved his broom aside: "Your step's gone light."

The seventh of the twelfth month: one day left before the date Zhou Heng named at the stewards' office door on the first of the eleventh. Tomorrow, Laba, the sect contest, inner court and outer court together, on the Five Elements Platform. Champion, one Foundation pill — one a year, for the whole temple.

exits._grant: 古五: the 鼎苔 moved to the 石室 (wm-xirang swallow, 2026-10-03: scraped clean, not a pinch); the stranger's dropped knife on the way back has no item of its own.
